If your goal is theory, then I can't recommend the book 'The Elements of Computing Systems' highly enough. It has you actually design a 4-bit CPU from the ground up, complete with an assembly language. Then you create a compiler for a C like language, and an operating system. It's incredible.

If you are looking for a more practical approach (probably learning x86 assembly), I would suggest grabbing a copy of NASM assembler, and start reading wikibooks, and hacking around.

Do you really need to learn assembly though? You can get almost as close to the metal using C.

MIPS is a great place to start. Start by learning how to write simple program in it. Next, move to writing a small parser for assembly that produces the actual binary. After that, write a small ALU that uses the binary to perform actual computation. Once you understand those primitive basics, look at something like the ARM instruction set and try to write some code in C / ARM. Then consider writing the lower half of a compiler, converting some higher-level language (even just BASIC) into assembly.

I started in the 1970's with the Z80 and the 6502. Assembly on those processors was easy due to the powerful but compact instruction set and hardware limitations. We had to work with assembly to optimise instruction execution cycles by hand. Later when I started with DSP's, hand optimising became a necessity due to the quality of the software tools available in the day.

Learning assembly for OS X is a whole different beast and a heck of a lot more complicated today than it was 40 years ago.

That said, it's fairly straightforward to get started with assembly on the Mac. You can use Xcode or the GNU compiler tools via command line, it's your choice.

I'd get started with the art of assembly language programming here: http://flint.cs.yale.edu/cs422/doc/art-of-asm/pdf/

Apple provides the OS X assembler reference here: https://developer.apple.com/library/mac/documentation/DeveloperTools/Reference/Assembler/000-Introduction/introduction.html

This book on OS X internals is a great reference: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/0321278542/

Ray's slides here can give you a concise summary of the highlights: http://rayseyfarth.com/asm/

Here's a sample hello world assembly application: http://peter.michaux.ca/articles/assembly-hello-world-for-os-x

This blog has a few useful insights: http://orangejuiceliberationfront.com/intel-assembler-on-mac-os-x/

And if you want a bit more on GCC assembly: http://www.ibiblio.org/gferg/ldp/GCC-Inline-Assembly-HOWTO.html

This is an old article but had some insights for me at the time: http://fabiensanglard.net/macosxassembly/index.php

I hope that can get you started and give you a taste of assembly.

Learn basic concepts first, like:

  • Register
  • Instruction
  • Jump
  • Conditional
  • Flag
  • Program Counter/Instruction Pointer
  • Address
  • Label
  • Section

Then, pick a real architecture (I recommend ARM, x86 is a mess), and start learning.

Realize that pure assembly language is:

  • learning the instruction set of the target architecture

  • understanding that everything you do is just moving data from one location to another

  • realizing you really should've done it in C instead
